sources.name: ESA Ocean Colour CCI v6.0: monthly climatology of remote-sensing reflectance (1997-2022)
sources.what: The sea's measured colour: reflectance (Rrs) at 412, 443, 490, 510, 560 and 665 nm, plus chlorophyll, merged from SeaWiFS, MODIS, MERIS, VIIRS and OLCI. About 4 km, one field per calendar month.
sources.improves: The sea (71 % of the globe's body) is now coloured only by depth zones (the SHELF/SLOPE/ABYSS/REEF hexes). Converting Rrs 443/560/665 to sRGB per month would give it its actual colour: green shelf seas, the brown Baltic, the muddy plumes of the Amazon, Yangtze and Rio de la Plata, spring blooms, and the milky turquoise coccolithophore blooms of the Barents and Bering seas. sources.name: ESA WorldCover 10 m 2021 v200 land cover, plus its Sentinel-2 RGBNIR annual composites, on AWS
sources.what: Eleven land-cover classes at 10 m (tree, shrub, grassland, cropland, built-up, bare/sparse, snow and ice, water, herbaceous wetland, mangroves, moss and lichen), plus the yearly cloud-free Sentinel-2 median composite the classes were made from.
sources.improves: build_material.py could blend each cell from its real class shares instead of inferring forest, grass or desert from biome, canopy height and aridity. It also adds what the globe lacks: cropland (not in CLASSES, yet the main surface of Europe, India and the US Midwest), shrubland, moss-and-lichen tundra, mangroves and exact built-up area. The RGBNIR composite gives each class its real local colour (Sahara red vs Arabian beige) for calibrating material colours.
sources.licence: CC BY 4.0. Credit: '© ESA WorldCover project 2021 / Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data (2021) processed by ESA WorldCover consortium'. Impact Observatory LULC is also CC BY 4.0.
sources.format: Class map: COG uint8, 3x3 degree tiles (36000x36000 px), overviews down to 562x562 (about 600 m). Composites: 1x1 degree, 4-band uint16 COGs (12000x12000 px, overviews down to 750x750) for 2020 and 2021. The swir/ and ndvi/ folders hold NDVI p10/p50/p90.
sources.notes: Already reachable; no redirects; no CORS (build-time only). Covers 2020/2021 only. For change through 2024, Impact Observatory's 10 m annual land cover (2017-2024, one file per UTM zone, CC BY 4.0, third host above) is also reachable. Class overviews are sampled, not averaged, so compute shares from a middle overview level (3-4). The same files on Planetary Computer and Terrascope (both blocked) are not needed.
sources.plan: Sampled 15 Oct 2026 through esa-worldcover.s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com with HTTP range requests (numpy and tifffile only): overview level 4 of 7 of a 3 degree tile (2,250 x 2,250 pixels, 148 m a pixel) is one 1 MB request, 1.5 to 2 s, and gives the class shares of a 39 km cell. Paris: built 52 %, tree 33 %, crop 8 %, grass 5 %, water 1 %. Ames, Iowa: crop 79 %, grass 9 %, tree 8 %, built 4 %. Manaus: tree 40 %, water 28 %, built 17 %, grass 12 %, wetland 3 %. Tamanrasset: bare 98.6 %. Kyoto: tree 60 %, built 25 %, water 6 %, crop 6 %. Next: build_material.py reads level 4 of each land tile once (about 2,600 tiles, about 2.6 GB, about 10 minutes eight at a time), reduces to the 1024 x 512 grid as shares of the eleven classes, and replaces the biome, canopy and aridity inference for forest, grass, desert and rock with them, adding cropland, shrub, moss and mangrove to CLASSES with the works' colours for them. Bigger than a small change (it changes how the globe is drawn): proposed, not built.

In the visitor's browser (CORS tiles), the globe could show today's real cloud and true colour, and the night side the actual Day/Night Band, under the real sun the page already computes.

sources.name: NOAA GMGSI: Global Mosaic of Geostationary Satellite Imagery (hourly), on AWS
sources.what: The whole world's clouds every hour: blended longwave IR, shortwave IR, water vapour and visible mosaics from Himawari-9, GOES-18/19 and Meteosat, about 40 minutes after the hour.
sources.improves: The globe's cloud is now a monthly climatology (DIRT's CERES-based cloud-*.webp). GMGSI's IR (cold means high, bright cloud), plus visible by day, gives the real cloud of the last hour under the real sun the page already computes (land.js sunNow), with storms where storms are. The page could fetch it directly (CORS *), or an hourly job could reduce it to a small WebP mask.
sources.licence: NOAA open data (NODD): free to use, attribution requested, no implied endorsement.
sources.format: NetCDF-4/HDF5 on a 4999x3000 grid (about 0.072 degrees, 8 km), 72.7S-72.7N, about 7 MB per band per hour. Path: GMGSI_{LW,SW,WV,VIS,SSR}/YYYY/MM/DD/HH/.
sources.notes: Already reachable; no redirects. Checked: hourly files up to 21 UTC today, Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *. Nothing beyond 72.7 degrees, so polar caps need the climatology. IR alone under-shows warm low cloud and fog, and visible exists only by day. Decoding in the browser needs an HDF5 reader (e.g. h5wasm), and 7 MB per visit is heavy on phones; a scheduled GitHub Action writing a ~100-200 KB alpha WebP would be lighter. Full-disk scans from noaa-goes19, noaa-goes18 and noaa-himawari9 (also reachable) give true-colour clouds by day, but at hundreds of MB per scan. The sun and terminator need no data: land.js's Almanac formula is already accurate to a fraction of a degree.

sources.what: Global land surface reflectance for 36 ten-day periods of 2020 (2019 has fewer bands), clouds removed and gaps interpolated, all Sentinel-2 bands at 120 m.

That replaces build_material.py's invented material colours (soil-class bare ground; CANOPY_*/GRASS/DRY_GRASS hexes mixed by aridity), so deserts, cropland, tundra, the seasonal green-up and winter snow look as they did. sources.licence: CC BY 4.0. Credit: 'Contains modified Copernicus data 2020 processed by Sentinel Hub'.
sources.format: COG uint16, one file per band per UTM grid zone, 647 zones per period, about 50 MB each. Internal overviews go down to 1/32 (about 3.8 km, e.g. 130x235 px). Path: YYYY/M/D/<zone>/<band>.tif, where D is the first day of the 10-day period. QM.tif is the quality mask.
sources.notes: Already reachable; no redirects; no CORS (build-time only). Covers land and coastal water only: no open ocean, and little or no Antarctica. One year only. Regions cloudy for long spells may keep cloud (QM flags them). The interpolation masks cloud only (CLM/CLP), so snow mostly survives, but bright snow taken for cloud gets interpolated over. Needs reprojection from UTM to equirectangular.

sources.name: World Bank 'Light Every Night': VIIRS Day/Night Band monthly global composites (NOAA/EOG processing), on AWS
sources.what: Measured night-light radiance for every month, Jan 2012 to Jun 2025 (Suomi NPP; NOAA-20 Jun 2023 to Feb 2025). Each month comes stray-light corrected or excluded, with a count of cloud-free nights.
sources.improves: Replaces the night side's invented lamps (land.js makeLights seeds random clusters on land) with the lights that are really there. A 12-month median of avg_rade9, reduced to the 1024x512 or 2048x1024 grid, gives each cell its true brightness: the Nile thread, the Trans-Siberian beads, Gulf flares, dark North Korea. Lamp colour can still come from the art palette.
sources.licence: CC BY 4.0 (World Bank open data licence). Credit: Light Every Night, World Bank / NOAA NCEI-EOG / University of Michigan.
sources.format: COG, float32 LZW, 15 arc-sec (86400x33601, 75N-65S), internal overviews down to 338x132. Each month is 3-4.5 GB, but the 2700x1051 or 5400x2101 overview is a few MB of range reads. CORS: Access-Control-Allow-Origin * (checked).
sources.notes: Already reachable from the session; no redirects. Monthly composites still contain short-lived light (fires, gas flares, fishing boats, aurora residue). Summer months above about 55 degrees are empty because of the midnight sun, so take a multi-month median of the slcorr files. The bucket's dated folders (YYYYMM/, npp_YYYYMM/) hold raw nightly swaths of 16-260 MB each; use only composites/.

sources.name: Municipal tree registers: New York, Boston, San Francisco, Seattle, Melbourne, Berlin (reachable now)
sources.what: Each city's own inventory of the trees it keeps: a record a tree, with its species (botanical and common name), trunk size, planting date where known and a point. New York: Parks' Forestry Tree Points (897,575 standing trees, updated 7 Oct 2026; 1,123,163 records with the retired and stumps) and the 2015 Street Tree Census (683,788). Berlin: Baumbestand, 434,765 street trees and 527,780 park trees, with planting year, age, crown diameter, trunk girth and height. San Francisco: Street Tree Inventory (144,491, updated 14 Oct 2026). Seattle: Combined Tree Point (240,255, with trunk diameter) and, from the University of Vermont's lidar read of 2021, 968,013 individual tree crowns (612,693 deciduous, 355,320 coniferous) with height, radius and type. Boston: BPRD Trees, park and street (55,227, updated 15 Oct 2026). Melbourne: Urban Forest trees with species and dimensions (82,064, with age and useful life).
sources.improves: The plants that rise round a character in a city come from DIRT's biome grammar, so every city of a biome gets the same few trees: New York and Boston the sugar maple, white oak, American beech, tulip tree and white pine; Berlin, Paris and Amsterdam the Palearctic beech, oak and hornbeam; Melbourne (and Sydney) New Zealand's tree ferns, southern beech, kahikatea and rimu; Seattle Douglas fir, western red cedar and Sitka spruce; San Francisco coast live oak and blue oak. The registers say what really stands there, counted. New York: London planetree 97,316, thornless honeylocust 71,366, pin oak 66,521, Callery pear 52,225, Japanese zelkova 33,111, littleleaf linden 27,538. Boston: honeylocust, littleleaf linden, Norway maple, red maple, pin oak. San Francisco: London plane, Brisbane box, New Zealand Christmas tree, swamp myrtle, southern magnolia. Seattle: Japanese maple, bigleaf maple, red maple, crabapple, Norway maple. Melbourne: river red gum, London plane, drooping sheoak, English elm, yellow box, black wattle, spotted gum. Berlin: linden is more than half of a 4,000-tree sample, then maple, plane, pear, horse chestnut, ash, oak. Seattle's lidar crowns are 37 % coniferous (355,320 of 968,013), so the grammar's firs and cedars are right for its canopy and wrong for its streets. With trunk size, height and crown diameter each species gets its real size, and Seattle's crown polygons give the canopy's shape and height from above, where a skyline's green cells ('g') now carry only Overture's land-use word, 'park' or 'garden'. Counted by cell, the registers would make a skyline's green the trees that are there.
sources.licence: All open, each credited by name. New York: NYC Open Data terms of use (no restriction; the datasets carry no licence field). San Francisco and Boston: Open Data Commons PDDL. Melbourne: CC BY. Berlin: Datenlizenz Deutschland Zero 2.0, and the WFS says 'no access restrictions'. sources.what: The Labeled Information Library of Alexandria's wildlife datasets on a public bucket: camera-trap stills with species labels, bounding boxes, timestamps and camera sites in COCO Camera Traps JSON, plus drone and aerial sets, about fifty datasets. ENA24 (9,676 images, 23 classes of the eastern US: American black bear 959 boxes, grey fox 438, red fox 413, white-tailed deer 381, coyote 344, bobcat 333, eastern grey squirrel 319, raccoon, opossum, skunk, wild turkey, crow); Idaho Camera Traps, Caltech Camera Traps and NACTI (North America; NACTI 3.7 million images); Snapshot Serengeti and Snapshot Safari (Africa); WCS Camera Traps (worldwide); Lindenthal (Cologne); Seattle-ish; Channel Islands (island fox); Orinoquia (Colombia); NZ Trailcams and Wellington; UNSW predators (Australia); desert lions (Namibia).
sources.improves: species.py's coats and proportions are typed by hand from Wikipedia's words, and the characters pass records that no photograph of the animal was reachable. These are the real animals in the field, in their ground. The median colour of the pixels inside a species' boxes (daytime frames: the infrared night frames are grey) gives its coat, pale belly and dark legs as photographed, by month where the timestamp is kept (the winter against the summer coat of a white-tailed deer or a coyote). A side-on box's aspect gives body depth against length, and 413 red fox boxes are a measured check on the fox sprite. The frame behind gives the leaf litter, grass and snow the animal stands in, which the plants that rise round it can match. Frame sequences show how the animal stands, trots and looks back.
sources.licence: Mostly the Community Data License Agreement, Permissive 1.0 (confirmed by secondary sources for ENA24, Snapshot Serengeti, Caltech Camera Traps and Wellington). Each dataset's page on lila.science (refused) holds its own licence and citation: read it before taking a dataset up. Photographs are reference only and never enter the repository; a measured colour or ratio may, with the dataset's credit.
sources.format: COCO Camera Traps JSON (images with file_name, width, height and, where kept, datetime and location; annotations with bbox [x, y, w, h] in pixels; categories): ENA24's is 3.8 MB. sources.name: Muybridge's Animal Locomotion plates: real gaits frame by frame (Library of Congress and the Met, public domain)
sources.what: Eadweard Muybridge's chronophotographs of animals in motion (1872-1887): 12 to 24 consecutive frames to a plate, with a distance scale. The Library of Congress lists 266 items for them in its photos search (collotype plates, albumen prints, the zoetrope strips): 'Deer, running' (1881: twelve frames of a stag), 'Deer, trotting', horses in every gait with and without a rider, ox, cow and bull, boar, goat, greyhound and dog, a cat leaping, an ostrich running, a hawk in flight, a raccoon, a sloth, a mule, a baboon climbing. The Met holds about ten public-domain plates and portfolios of them, each object with many plate images.
sources.improves: The characters' gaits are drawn from stated rules (a trot in four frames at six a second; gait_feet and stand_feet in each plan), and the characters pass checks 'which feet are down in which frame' against the real animal with no real frames to hand. Muybridge's plates are the real frames: a deer's, ox's, boar's, goat's, greyhound's (the CANID gallop), cat's (the FELID leap), ostrich's (RATITE), hawk's (RAPTOR) and horse's (EQUID) feet and spine through a stride, with the bend of each leg at each phase, and a clean side-on silhouette of the animal's proportions. Nearly every body plan in rigs.py has a plate that fits it.
sources.licence: Public domain: Muybridge died in 1904 and the plates date from 1872 to 1887. The Library of Congress gives 'no known restrictions on publication'; the Met's Open Access images are CC0. Credit the holder.
sources.format: Library of Congress: JSON (www.loc.gov/photos/?q=...&fo=json: title, date, image URLs), JPEG on tile.loc.gov in sizes (_150px, v = 1,024 px, r = full). The Met: JSON API (search, objects with primaryImage and additionalImages), JPEG on images.metmuseum.org (web-large 600 px, original).
sources.notes: Sampled 15 Oct 2026: LOC's /photos/ JSON (266 hits for 'muybridge animal locomotion') and one plate ('Deer, running', 1881, 1,024 x 818, 104 KB) through tile.loc.gov; the Met's /v1.1/search for his public-domain plates (23 hits, ten of them his) and two plates (a horse and rider jumping, 600 px) through images.metmuseum.org. www.loc.gov's robots.txt disallows /search and /pictures/search and asks for a 5 second crawl delay: use /photos/ or /collections/ and wait 5 seconds between requests. tile.loc.gov has no robots.txt and answers 403 to curl's default User-Agent and to its bare root, but 200 to a descriptive User-Agent. The 'Animal locomotion' plates' titles are numbers (65 items): the animal is in the plate, not the title. The complete 781 plates (Penn's, the Internet Archive's) need *.us.archive.org, already on the later list for BHL. sources.what: Tobias et al. 2022 (Ecology Letters): morphological traits measured on 90,020 individuals of 11,009 bird species from 181 countries, with species means on three taxonomies: beak length (culmen and nares), beak width and depth, tarsus, wing, Kipps distance, secondary, hand-wing index, tail length and mass; with ecological and range data.

AVONET gives the real beak, tarsus, tail and wing ratios of the species actually drawn (the bald eagle, starling, greylag goose, crane, macaw), so a stubby goose bill or a long heron leg is the measured one and every generated bird can be checked at once.
sources.licence: Open. The paper is open access (CC BY); the data record on figshare (doi 10.6084/m9.figshare.16586228) states its own licence, to confirm on the record (not reachable from the session). Cite Tobias et al. 2022, doi 10.1111/ele.13898.

sources.name: Tree Species Germany (DLR): dominant tree species at 10 m, 2016 and 2022
sources.what: A map of the dominant tree species of Germany at 10 m, from Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 time series with phenology and 80,000 to 100,000 training samples (urban tree inventories, Street View and field work among them): ten classes, 0 pine, 1 spruce, 2 Douglas fir, 3 larch, 4 fir, 5 beech, 6 oak, 7 birch, 8 alder, 9 other (2022: 666 canopy cover loss; 2016: other deciduous and 800 uncertain). sources.improves: The plants that rise round a character in Berlin, Munich, Cologne, Dusseldorf and Hamburg come from DIRT's biome grammar, which plants every Palearctic broadleaf city with the same beech and hazel. This says what stands: the class shares inside a 5 km tile of Grunewald (read 20 Oct 2026) are pine 28 %, oak 19 %, larch 7 %, birch 7 %, beech 4 %, the rest not forest, which is Brandenburg's pine and oak, not beech and hazel. A planting can be counted from the map's shares round a city's point, not guessed from a biome. Also a real second colour for the forests of the globe's cells in Germany (pine dark, larch and birch bright).
sources.licence: CC BY 4.0 (each readme states it); credit DLR EOC (ForstEO). Contact named in the readme: Marco Wegler, DLR.
sources.format: Cloud-optimised GeoTIFF (BigTIFF, LZW, 512 px tiles, 8 overviews), ETRS89 / LAEA Europe (EPSG:3035), uint16, 10 m: 65,270 x 88,222 px (width x height), 524 MiB (2022) and 538 MiB (2016); a QGIS style file and a readme beside each.
sources.notes: On a host the site already reads (download.geoservice.dlr.de, for WSF-Evolution). sources.improves: Sydney is the artist's own city and the characters pass's standing gap: DIRT's grammar has no eucalypts for its biome, so a wave there raises New Zealand's tree ferns, southern beech, kahikatea and rimu. Counting the recent native records within ~10 km of the city's point gives the plants that are really there (to be counted, not guessed: eucalypts, angophoras, banksias and the rest), and the same for its native animal (the character's species is chosen from what the records show beside the grammar's list). A photograph per species, with its licence, would give the real coat, plumage and leaf colour to measure (median Lab of the pixels inside the animal) instead of hexes typed from Wikipedia's words. sources.name: Natural-history museum specimen photographs: NHM London Data Portal and Naturalis Bioportal
sources.what: Two museums' collections as open APIs. The Natural History Museum (London) Data Portal is a CKAN site at data.nhm.ac.uk with a keyless JSON API (base https://data.nhm.ac.uk/api/3): millions of specimen records, many with photographs; dataset metadata CC0, media by default CC BY (check each record's licence). The Naturalis Biodiversity Data Service (api.biodiversitydata.nl/v2, documented at docs.biodiversitydata.nl) serves Naturalis's digitised collection: specimens and over five million photographs, keyless; images from medialib.naturalis.nl.
sources.improves: A real animal or plant as a museum photographed it, in even light against a plain ground: a bird's study skin, a mammal's pelt, a pressed leaf or an insect's wings, by species and sex. The coat and plumage colours that species.py types by hand, and the markings (an ocellated lizard's blue ocelli, a squirrel's ear tufts), can be measured and checked at once for the 118 generated species and the eight drawn by hand. Specimens fade and are lit studio-white, so they check colour and pattern and do not set them (as the Smithsonian's study skins do).
sources.licence: NHM: dataset metadata CC0; multimedia by default CC BY and (c) the Trustees of the Natural History Museum, London, each dataset's licence field governs (a few CC BY-NC). Naturalis: open content policy, non-restrictive licences, the licence on each media record (CC0, CC BY, CC BY-NC seen in its object model: filter). Read colours and counts only; credit the museum.
sources.format: JSON (CKAN action API: package_search, datastore_search by resource; NBA: specimen/query and multimedia/query with a JSON querySpec); JPEG media.
sources.notes: Not sampled (hosts refused). The NHM site's terms and 'no key needed' are from its own credits and API pages; the NBA endpoint is from its documentation index and the nbaR client, and was not confirmed by a request. GBIF's occurrence API (already open) also lists specimen media from both museums, with the museum's host in each URL: those hosts are what a script would need whichever route it takes. sources.name: USDA Forest Service Urban Tree Database (and TreeMap 2016): the size and crown of city trees
sources.what: McPherson, van Doorn and Peper (2016, PSW-GTR-253; RDS-2016-0005, DOI 10.2737/RDS-2016-0005): measurements of over 14,000 street and park trees in 17 cities of 13 states, 1998-2012, and 365 sets of allometric equations (eight each, for about 20 common species in 16 climate regions): age gives trunk diameter, and trunk diameter gives height, crown diameter, crown height and leaf area. The same archive holds TreeMap 2016 (a tree list for every 30 m pixel of the United States, from the Forest Inventory and Analysis plots; RDS-2021-0074, number not confirmed).
sources.improves: New York's, San Francisco's and Boston's tree registers (already open) give species and trunk diameter but no crown. These equations give each tree its crown height and width from its trunk and species, so the plants that rise round a character in those cities, and a skyline's green cells ('g'), are drawn at the size the registers' trees really are: a London planetree is not a honeylocust. A second use: leaf area index by species for the canopy's density.
sources.licence: Archive terms: 'data were collected using funding from the U.S. Government and can be used without additional permissions or fees' (a US federal work; the archive's own wording, not read from here: check the record's metadata). Cite McPherson et al. 2016.
sources.format: CSV (field data, equation coefficients), a PDF report and an errata file (January 2020, which corrects the data and the report: apply it); delivered as one zip from the archive.
sources.notes: Not sampled: www.fs.usda.gov is refused. The probe address is the archive's product page, found by search; the data zip's address is not seen. A mirror on Ag Data Commons (agdatacommons.nal.usda.gov, article 27006565) is also refused here. The search results did not say whether crown shape is a field (do not assume it is): the equations give size, not form. The cities' registers' trunk diameter classes make the join: species first, then DBH.

sources.name: USGS Spectral Library Version 7: measured reflectance of leaves, grasses, soils, rocks and building materials
sources.what: Laboratory, field and airborne reflectance spectra (from the ultraviolet to the thermal infrared) of minerals, rocks, soils, man-made materials and vegetation, with plant material at leaf and plant level for single species and as field spectra of mixed plots (Louisiana's coastal wetlands) and, for forests too tall for a field spectrometer, airborne spectra of plots; DOI 10.5066/F7RR1WDJ on ScienceBase; native SPECPR, plus generic text files of the spectra and metadata.
sources.improves: A spectrum, run through the visible bands and the CIE colour-matching functions, is a measured colour: what a green leaf, a dry grass, a bare soil, a sandstone or a roofing slate really reflects, with no camera, light or model in between. The globe's body (build_material.py) mixes invented hexes (CANOPY_*, GRASS, DRY_GRASS, the bare soils) by aridity; each can be replaced by the colour of a sampled spectrum, and the plants' look in the characters pass and the building materials of the models likewise. It is the lab check against the satellite and photograph readings (Sentinel-2, MODIS, iNaturalist).
sources.licence: CC0 1.0 Universal as the ScienceBase record is reported to mark it (search result 20 Oct 2026; confirm on the item's rights field). Cite Kokaly et al. 2017, USGS Data Series 1035.
sources.format: SPECPR binary and generic ASCII text files (one file per spectrum and per instrument/wavelength set), metadata in text; downloaded as zips from the ScienceBase item.
sources.notes: Not sampled: www.sciencebase.gov and pubs.usgs.gov are refused. The ScienceBase item is 5807a2a2e4b0841e59e3a18d (JSON at /catalog/item/<id>?format=json lists its files and sizes). A reflectance spectrum is under lit conditions of the laboratory, not a landscape's: leaf-level greens are saturated beside what a canopy shows from space, so use it to check hue and relative lightness, not to replace the canopy's colour. JPL's ECOSTRESS spectral library (speclib.jpl.nasa.gov; it includes USGS spectra) was considered and left out: its pages carry 'Copyright 2017 California Institute of Technology, all rights reserved' and ordering is by form (up to a week), with no licence found; the USGS library is the open part of it. 21 Oct 2026: the whole-library zip (5.5 GB) is on sciencebase.usgs.gov, refused; its children are smaller and on www.sciencebase.gov itself.

sources.name: Global Mangrove Watch v3: mangrove extent, 1996-2020, at 25 m
sources.what: Mangrove extent mapped from radar and optical satellite data for eleven epochs between 1996 and 2020 (1996, 2007-2010, 2015-2020), at 25 m, as vector polygons and rasters: 147,359 km2 in 2020, 3.4 % lost since 1996.
sources.improves: Where the tropical coast is green. The globe draws a coast by its biome and a wetland flag; Global Mangrove Watch puts the mangrove where it stands (the Sundarbans, the Niger and Mekong deltas, Florida's coast, northern Australia, the Brazilian coast), and a coastal city's planting can hold mangrove where the extent says so (Miami, Mumbai, Sydney's Parramatta River). The epochs show the loss to ponds and clearing as a change of colour over time.
sources.licence: CC BY 4.0 (the Zenodo record page, read 23 Oct 2026: 'Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International'); credit Bunting et al. 2022, Remote Sensing 14(15), and the Global Mangrove Watch.

sources.name: Vienna's Franciscan cadastre (c. 1829): every plot's land use and every building, Stadt Wien open data
sources.what: The city's own digitisation of the Franziszeischer Kataster, Vienna's first cadastral survey: 102,125 polygons with a land-use class, TYP (Acker 20,309; Stein 16,642; Obstgarten 10,422; Holz 10,410; WieseT 8,884; Wein 7,469; Gemuese 6,885; Ziergarten 6,081; Park 3,325; Laubwald, Boeschung, Weideland, Militaer, Bruecke, Bach, Kirche 210, Linienwall 96 ...), as a WFS (ogdwien:FRANZKATOGD, native EPSG:31256: ask srsName=EPSG:4326) and a WMS layer (FRANZKATOGD) at data.wien.gv.at/daten/geo, the endpoint the site already reads for Vienna's building periods. By polygon size on a sample, Stein (median 211 m2, 348 sampled) is masonry buildings, Holz (median 41 m2, 399 sampled) timber sheds and houses, Kirche 179 m2, Laubwald (9,313 m2) woods. The layer's date field (SE_ANNO_CAD_DATA) is empty: the survey's year is not in the data.
sources.improves: Vienna's dial begins with periods (before 1683, 1683-1740, 1741-1780 ...) and all unbuilt land one green. This is what the ground was before the city came out over it: the vineyards (Wein), fields (Acker), orchards and gardens round the Linienwall, the open Glacis round the old city and its bastions, the Danube's arms, each building of 1829 stone or timber. The skyline's earliest years can stand on that ground, its not-yet-built cells given their own colour, and the building periods checked against which footprints stood. A GetMap of the inner city (16.360-16.385 E, 48.205-48.215 N, 800x320) drew the walled city, the bastions and glacis, the Danube Canal and no Ringstrasse.

The WMS draws all classes in grey and black: take the polygons, not the picture. The same service lists 753 layers; none is a historical orthophoto (no LUFTBILD, no 1938 or 1956).

sources.name: Global map of Local Climate Zones (Demuzere et al. 2022; version 3.0.0, 2023), 100 m, on Zenodo
sources.what: Every land cell of the Earth at 100 m in one of the 17 Local Climate Zone classes: ten built types (compact high-rise, mid-rise and low-rise; open high-rise, mid-rise and low-rise; lightweight low-rise; large low-rise; sparsely built; heavy industry) and seven natural (dense trees, scattered trees, bush, low plants, bare rock or paved, bare soil or sand, water), from multiple Earth-observation datasets and expert-labelled training areas, with a probability layer. Zenodo record 8419340 (8 Oct 2023): lcz_v3.tif 1.76 GB, lcz_filter_v3.tif 1.38 GB, lcz_probability_v3.tif 8.9 GB, a 1.5 MB preview PNG and a readme.
sources.improves: What a city's blocks are made of where no footprints exist. The skyline draws buildings from Overture, thin over much of Latin America, Africa and South and Southeast Asia (Mexico City, Buenos Aires and Mumbai are named in this ledger as places with no city record). The class tells Mexico City's compact mid-rise centre from its open low-rise hillsides and the large low-rise roofs of its warehouses and markets, so a missing district can stand as dense or open, tall or low, with a typical share of roof, paving and trees (Stewart and Oke 2012), instead of bare ground; and the globe's 'city' ground could take its colour from the built type, not one grey (URBAN_GROUND #8a8277).
sources.licence: CC BY 4.0 (the Zenodo record page, read 23 Oct 2026, and its readme). The readme asks that the authors and the WUDAPT contributors be credited, and says the data come from crowd-sourcing and machine learning, with errors and no warranty. Cite Demuzere M, Kittner J, Martilli A, et al. 2022, Earth System Science Data 14(8), 3835-3873, doi 10.5194/essd-14-3835-2022.
sources.format: BigTIFF, 256 px tiles, LZW, one 8-bit class band, about 389,620 x 155,995 px (first IFD read); Range requests answer 206; the tile tables are in the first 11 MB (tags at 3.7 MB and 11.1 MB), so a city's window costs that head read and then its tiles
sources.notes: Hosted on zenodo.org, newly open 23 Oct 2026. Zenodo's robots.txt: Disallow /search, /api, /records/*/preview; Allow /api/records/*/files; Crawl-delay 10. So the record page, the file list (/api/records/8419340/files) and the files (/api/records/8419340/files/lcz_v3.tif/content) are read, one request in ten seconds; never /search or /api/records/<id>. Version 2.0.0 (record 7324909) and the first (6364594) are older. The LCZ classes say how a place is built, not what colour it is.
sources.plan: Sampled 23 Oct 2026 under Zenodo's robots.txt, one request in eleven seconds: the record page (licence cc-by-4.0, version 3.0.0, 8 Oct 2023), the file list (5 files), readme.txt (7.7 kB) and a Range read of lcz_v3.tif's first 64 kB (206, 'bytes 0-65535/1758460544'; a BigTIFF, tiled 256, LZW; its tile offset tables lie further in, so no window was read).
